lessons.title: Identifying Termite and Pest Damage
lessons.body:
Termites and other pests can silently destroy a building from the inside out. In Africa, the most common culprits are subterranean termites (especially the genera Macrotermes and Odontotermes), drywood termites, and carpenter ants. Subterranean termites build mud tubes on foundation walls, pillars, and wooden structures. These tubes are about the thickness of a pencil and are made of soil, saliva, and feces. Break a tube open: if you see soft, creamy-white worker termites, you have an active infestation. Drywood termites leave tiny holes (1-2 mm) in wood and push out six-sided fecal pellets that look like coarse sand. Carpenter ants don't eat wood but tunnel through it, leaving sawdust-like frass. Other pests include powderpost beetles, which reduce wood to powder, and rodents, which gnaw on wires and pipes.

To inspect, use a bright torch, a flat-head screwdriver, and a notebook. Tap wood with the screwdriver handle: a hollow sound means internal damage. Probe soft spots gently. Check dark, damp areas: under sinks, behind baseboards, in roof voids, and around foundations. Look for mud tubes, discarded wings (after swarming), and bubbling paint or wallpaper. In Africa, termite swarms often happen after the first heavy rains. If you see winged termites emerging from a crack in your wall, that's a swarm. Take photos and note locations.

Quantify the damage: measure the length of mud tubes, count exit holes per square meter, and note any sagging floors or doors that no longer close. A simple test: push an awl into wood; if it sinks more than 5 mm with little resistance, the wood is compromised. For a small fee, local extension officers or pest control companies can confirm species. Early detection saves thousands: treating a small infestation might cost 50-100 USD, while replacing a roof can cost 2,000 USD or more. Always wear gloves and a dust mask when inspecting, as termite dust and rodent droppings can carry disease.

lessons.title: Chemical and Natural Termite Barriers
lessons.body:
A termite barrier is a continuous physical or chemical shield that stops termites from reaching your building. In Africa, you have two main options: chemical soil treatments and physical or natural barriers. For chemical barriers, the most common active ingredients are imidacloprid (e.g., Premise), fipronil (e.g., Termidor), and bifenthrin. These are mixed with water and applied to the soil around the foundation at a rate of 1-2 liters per square meter, depending on the product label. The goal is to create a treated zone 10-15 cm wide and at least 30 cm deep around all foundation walls, pillars, and plumbing penetrations. You need a watering can or a low-pressure sprayer, a measuring cup, and personal protective equipment (gloves, goggles, mask). Always follow the label: overdosing wastes money and harms the environment; underdosing fails.

Natural barriers are cheaper and safer for families. Sand barriers: termites cannot tunnel through uniform sand particles larger than 1.5 mm. Create a 10 cm layer of washed river sand (not fine sand) around the foundation. Diatomaceous earth (DE) is a powder made from fossilized algae; it scratches the termite's exoskeleton, causing dehydration. Apply a 5 cm band of DE around foundations and in wall voids. Keep it dryâwet DE is ineffective. Neem oil or neem cake: mix 200 g of neem cake per 10 liters of water and drench the soil. Neem is a natural repellent. For existing buildings, you can also use a physical barrier like stainless steel mesh (Termi-Mesh) over foundation cracks and vents, but this is expensive. A cheaper physical barrier is crushed granite (particles 2-4 mm) packed around pipes.

In Africa, many builders combine methods: a chemical barrier for immediate protection and a sand or DE barrier for long-term, low-cost maintenance. Reapply chemical barriers every 5-10 years, or after flooding. Natural barriers need reapplication every 1-2 years. Always store chemicals in a locked cabinet away from children and food. If you cannot afford commercial products, focus on sand and DE barriers, and keep soil dryâtermites love moisture.

lessons.title: Treating Infested Wood and Soil
lessons.body:
Once termites or pests have infested wood or soil, you must treat both to stop the colony. For wood, you have three main approaches: injection, surface spraying, and fumigation. Injection is best for structural timbers (roof trusses, door frames). Drill 6-8 mm holes every 30-40 cm along the wood, angled downward, and inject a termiticide like fipronil or imidacloprid using a syringe or a pressure sprayer with a needle attachment. Use about 10-20 ml of mixed solution per hole. For surface spraying, mix a 0.5% solution of bifenthrin or permethrin and spray all exposed wood until it drips. Repeat after 2 weeks. For severe infestations, fumigation with sulfuryl fluoride or methyl bromide is done by professionals; it kills all stages of termites but requires sealing the building and evacuating for 24-48 hours. This is expensive (500-2000 USD) and rarely used in rural Africa.

For soil treatment, you need to create a chemical barrier in the soil around and under the building. Dig a trench 30 cm deep and 15 cm wide along the foundation. Mix 5 liters of termiticide concentrate (e.g., 2% fipronil) with 100 liters of water, and pour the solution into the trench at a rate of 5 liters per meter. Backfill immediately. For active mounds near the building, destroy the mound by digging it out and drenching the soil with the same solution. If you find termites inside a wall, drill holes every 30 cm at floor level and inject insecticide foam (like Termidor Foam) into the void. Foam expands and coats surfaces.

Natural treatments: Borate wood preservatives (e.g., borax and boric acid mixed with water) are effective and low-toxicity. Mix 1 part borax, 1 part boric acid, and 10 parts water. Brush or spray onto bare wood; it penetrates and kills termites on contact. For soil, drench with a neem oil solution (10 ml neem oil per liter of water) every 3 months. Always wear gloves, goggles, and a mask when handling any pesticide. Ventilate the area during and after treatment. Keep children and pets away until dry. After treatment, monitor monthly for new mud tubes or frass.

lessons.title: Preventive Design: Keeping Pests Out
lessons.body:
The cheapest way to control termites and pests is to design and build so they cannot enter. Start with the foundation. Use concrete or steel instead of wood for any ground-contact structural elements. If you must use wood, choose naturally resistant species like teak, iroko, or mahogany, or pressure-treated timber. In Africa, many local hardwoods are termite-resistant. Elevate the building: a minimum 45 cm clearance between the ground and the lowest wooden floor. This allows inspection and keeps wood dry. Ensure proper drainage: slope the ground away from the building at a 5% grade, and install gutters and downspouts to carry water at least 1.5 meters away. Fix leaking taps and pipes immediatelyâmoisture attracts termites.

During construction, install a physical barrier before pouring the slab. Use a 0.5 mm thick plastic sheet (vapor barrier) under the slab, and seal all joints. For walls, use concrete blocks filled with concrete and rebar; termites can tunnel through hollow blocks. Seal cracks and gaps around pipes, wires, and windows with mortar or silicone caulk. Avoid wood-to-ground contact: use metal brackets or concrete plinths to raise wooden posts. For roofs, use metal or concrete trusses instead of wood. If using wood, treat it with borate before installation. Keep vegetation trimmed: bushes and trees should be at least 1 meter from the walls, as they provide bridges and moisture. Remove any dead wood, stumps, or cardboard boxes from around the building.

In existing buildings, you can retrofit preventive measures. Install stainless steel mesh over foundation vents and weep holes. Use sand or crushed granite barriers as described in Lesson 2. Keep the perimeter dry: fix leaks, improve ventilation in crawl spaces, and remove mulch that touches the foundation. Store firewood and timber off the ground on concrete blocks, away from the house. In Africa, many families store grain and food in the house; use sealed plastic or metal containers, not cardboard or paper. Regularly inspect your building, especially after rains. A 30-minute inspection every month can catch a problem before it costs thousands. Remember: termites need food (wood), moisture, and shelter. Deny them any one of these, and you prevent infestation.

lessons.title: Safe Handling and Application of Pesticides
lessons.body:
Pesticides are poisons. They kill termites, but they can also harm you, your family, and your livestock if misused. Always read the label before opening any container. The label tells you the active ingredient, the mixing ratio, the safety precautions, and the first aid measures. Never transfer pesticides into food or drink containers. Store them in a locked cabinet, away from children, pets, and food. Wear personal protective equipment (PPE): long-sleeved shirt, long trousers, closed shoes, rubber gloves, goggles, and a dust mask or respirator. For fumigants, you need a full-face respirator with the correct cartridge. Do not eat, drink, or smoke while handling pesticides. Mix only the amount you need, outdoors or in a well-ventilated area. Use a dedicated measuring cup and stirring stickânever use kitchen utensils.

Apply pesticides carefully. For soil drenches, pour slowly along the foundation, avoiding runoff into storm drains or wells. Keep people and animals away from the treated area for at least 24 hours, or as the label states. For indoor spraying, cover furniture, remove food, and open windows after application. Never spray against the wind. If you spill concentrate, absorb it with sand or sawdust, then shovel it into a sealed container for safe disposal. Do not wash spillage into drains. After handling, wash your hands, face, and clothes separately from other laundry. Take a shower. If you feel dizzy, nauseous, or have trouble breathing, get fresh air and seek medical help immediately. Bring the pesticide label with you.

Dispose of empty containers safely: triple-rinse them, puncture them, and bury them at least 50 cm deep, away from water sources. Never reuse pesticide containers. In Africa, many people use empty pesticide bottles for water or oilâthis causes poisoning. Buy pesticides from licensed agro-dealers, not from open markets where products may be fake or expired. Check the expiry date. If you cannot afford commercial pesticides, use natural alternatives like neem, diatomaceous earth, or borate solutions. These are safer but still require care. For any large infestation, hire a licensed pest control operator. They have training, equipment, and insurance. The cost is worth it: a professional treatment might cost 200-500 USD, but it protects your family and your building.

lessons.title: Case Study: Saving a Building from Termite Infestation
lessons.body:
In 2019, a community center in Kisumu, Kenya, faced collapse. The building had a wooden roof truss and wooden door frames. After two years of heavy rains, staff noticed sagging ceilings, doors that wouldn't close, and mud tubes on the foundation. An inspection revealed active subterranean termites (Macrotermes) and drywood termites in the roof. The damage was severe: 30% of the roof truss was hollow, and the main door frame was crumbling. The estimated repair cost was 8,000 USDâmore than the annual budget. The community decided to act fast and cheaply.

First, they hired a local pest control officer for 150 USD to confirm the species and map the infestation. The officer found mud tubes every 2 meters along the foundation and frass under the roof. The community then bought fipronil concentrate (Termidor) for 120 USD and treated the soil: they dug a 30 cm trench around the building, mixed 100 ml of concentrate with 10 liters of water, and poured it at 5 liters per meter. They also drilled holes into the remaining sound wood and injected a 0.5% fipronil solution. For the roof, they removed all damaged timber and replaced it with pressure-treated pine (cost: 1,200 USD). They installed a stainless steel mesh over foundation vents (200 USD) and applied borate solution to all new wood (50 USD).

Total cost: about 1,720 USDâfar less than 8,000 USD. The community also made preventive changes: they cleared vegetation 1 meter from the walls, fixed a leaking pipe, and installed gutters. They now inspect every month. Two years later, no new termite activity. The key lessons: act quickly, combine chemical and physical barriers, replace damaged wood with treated timber, and involve a professional for diagnosis. The community also trained two members as pest monitors, who check for mud tubes and frass. This case shows that even a low-budget building can be saved if you follow the methods in this module.

quiz.q: What is the most common sign of subterranean termites?
quiz.explanation: Subterranean termites build mud tubes to travel from soil to wood.

quiz.q: Which tool is best for probing soft wood during an inspection?
quiz.explanation: A flat-head screwdriver can gently probe for hollow or soft spots.

quiz.q: What does a hollow sound when tapping wood indicate?
quiz.explanation: Hollow sounds suggest termites have eaten the wood from inside.

quiz.q: Which termite species leaves six-sided fecal pellets?
quiz.explanation: Drywood termites push out six-sided pellets that look like coarse sand.

quiz.q: What is the recommended depth for a chemical soil barrier trench?
quiz.explanation: A 30 cm deep trench ensures the chemical reaches the termite travel zone.

quiz.q: Which natural barrier works by scratching the termite's exoskeleton?
quiz.explanation: Diatomaceous earth is abrasive and causes dehydration.

quiz.q: How often should chemical termite barriers be reapplied?
quiz.explanation: Most chemical barriers degrade and need reapplication every 5-10 years.

quiz.q: What is the active ingredient in Termidor?
quiz.explanation: Termidor contains fipronil as its active ingredient.

quiz.q: Which method is best for treating structural timbers?
quiz.explanation: Injection delivers insecticide deep into the wood where termites live.

quiz.q: What is the mixing ratio for a borate wood preservative?
options: A) 1 part borax, 1 part boric acid, 10 parts water
B) 1 part borax, 10 parts boric acid, 1 part water
C) 10 parts borax, 1 part boric acid, 1 part water
D) 1 part borax, 1 part boric acid, 1 part water
quiz.explanation: The standard mix is 1:1:10 borax, boric acid, and water.

quiz.q: How deep should you drill holes for wood injection?
quiz.explanation: 6-8 mm holes are large enough for the injector but small enough to patch.

quiz.q: What is the recommended spacing between injection holes?
quiz.explanation: 30-40 cm spacing ensures the insecticide spreads throughout the wood.

quiz.q: Which of these is a natural soil treatment for termites?
quiz.explanation: Neem oil is a natural repellent that can be drenched into soil.

quiz.q: What is the minimum clearance between ground and wooden floor?
quiz.explanation: 45 cm clearance allows inspection and keeps wood dry.

quiz.q: What slope should the ground have away from a building?
quiz.explanation: A 5% slope directs water away from the foundation.

quiz.q: Which material is best for a physical termite barrier under a slab?
quiz.explanation: A plastic vapor barrier also acts as a physical termite barrier.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid wood-to-ground contact?
quiz.explanation: Wood-to-ground contact gives termites direct access to food.

quiz.q: How far should vegetation be kept from walls?
quiz.explanation: 1 meter prevents plants from bridging to the building and reducing airflow.

quiz.q: What should you wear when handling pesticides?
options: C) Full PPE including gloves, goggles, and mask
quiz.explanation: Full PPE protects against skin contact, inhalation, and eye splashes.

quiz.q: Where should pesticides be stored?
options: B) In a locked cabinet away from food
quiz.explanation: Locked storage prevents accidental poisoning, especially of children.

quiz.q: What should you do if you spill pesticide concentrate?
options: A) Wash it into the drain
B) Absorb with sand and dispose safely
quiz.explanation: Absorbing and proper disposal prevents environmental contamination.

quiz.q: How long should people stay away from a treated area?
quiz.explanation: Most labels require 24 hours before re-entry.

quiz.q: What is the first thing to do if you feel dizzy after pesticide exposure?
options: B) Get fresh air and seek medical help
quiz.explanation: Fresh air and medical attention are critical for pesticide poisoning.

quiz.q: How should you dispose of empty pesticide containers?
quiz.explanation: Triple-rinsing and burying prevents reuse and environmental harm.

quiz.q: In the case study, what was the total cost of saving the building?
quiz.explanation: The community spent about 1,720 USD, far less than the 8,000 USD repair estimate.

quiz.q: What chemical did the community use for soil treatment?
quiz.explanation: They used fipronil (Termidor) for the soil barrier.

quiz.q: What was the first step the community took?
options: B) Hired a pest control officer
quiz.explanation: They hired a professional to confirm the species and map the infestation.

quiz.q: Which preventive measure did the community add after treatment?
quiz.explanation: They fixed leaks and installed gutters to reduce moisture.

quiz.q: How often did the community inspect after treatment?
quiz.explanation: Monthly inspections help catch new activity early.

quiz.q: What is the main lesson from the case study?
options: B) Acting quickly and combining methods saves money
quiz.explanation: Early action and a combination of chemical and physical barriers saved the building.
